cluster.name: Rishikesh-Haridwar
cluster.summary: Twin Ganga towns at the point where the river leaves the Himalaya for the plains: Haridwar for pilgrimage and the Har Ki Pauri aarti, Rishikesh for yoga, whitewater rafting and forested riverside walks. About 25 km apart.

attractions.name: Har Ki Pauri & Ganga Aarti
attractions.summary: The principal bathing ghat of Haridwar, believed to bear Vishnu's footprint, and site of the evening Ganga Aarti.
attractions.history: Tradition holds that Vishnu left a footprint on a stone here, and that a drop of amrita fell at this spot during the churning of the ocean - which is why Haridwar is one of the four Kumbh Mela cities. King Vikramaditya is credited with building the ghat in memory of his brother Bhartrihari. The present embankments were substantially rebuilt in the twentieth century.
attractions.significance: Har Ki Pauri is the ritual centre of Haridwar and the focal point of the Kumbh Mela held here every twelve years. Its evening aarti, with lamps floated downstream on leaf boats, is among the most-attended daily rituals in India.
interesting_facts: The name means 'footsteps of the Lord', referring to Vishnu's footprint on a stone at the ghat.
Haridwar is one of only four cities that host the Kumbh Mela.
Diyas floated on the river after aarti are made from leaves and marigold, and are set adrift by the current.
Chains are fixed along the bathing steps because the current here is genuinely strong.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The upper promenade is level and reachable, and gives a usable view of the aarti. Descending to the water requires steps that are wet and slippery.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear must be removed near the ghat steps.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography of the aarti is permitted. Do not photograph people bathing, particularly women.
local_customs: Hold the fixed chains if you enter the water - the current is dangerous.
Alcohol and non-vegetarian food are prohibited throughout Haridwar.
Priests may request a donation after applying a tilak - agree an amount beforehand or decline politely.
Arrive 45 minutes early for the evening aarti.

schedule.note: Public ghat; aarti at sunrise and sunset

attractions.verification_note: Aarti timing follows sunset and shifts through the year - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Lakshman Jhula & Tera Manzil Temple
attractions.summary: The iron suspension footbridge over the Ganga at Rishikesh's northern end, beside the tiered Tera Manzil temple.
attractions.history: Tradition holds that Lakshmana, brother of Rama, crossed the Ganga at this point on a jute-rope bridge. A suspension bridge was built in 1889 and rebuilt in iron in 1929 after floods. The historic bridge was closed to pedestrians on safety grounds in 2019 and a replacement crossing was built nearby; the area around it remains the focal point of northern Rishikesh.
attractions.significance: The crossing anchors the temple and ashram quarter of Rishikesh, and the thirteen-storey Tera Manzil (Trayambakeshwar) temple beside it gives the best elevated view of the river gorge. The bridge itself has been the visual shorthand for Rishikesh for a century.
interesting_facts: The thirteen-storey Tera Manzil temple houses shrines to many deities across its levels, reached by stairs.
The original 1889 bridge was washed away in floods in 1924.
The 1929 iron bridge was closed to the public in 2019 on structural safety grounds.
The top level of Tera Manzil gives an unobstructed view up the Ganga gorge.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Approach lanes are narrow with steps, and the temple is a stair climb of thirteen levels with no lift. Not wheelchair accessible.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear removed inside the temple.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography permitted outdoors; sanctum photography inside the temple is restricted.
local_customs: Watch for monkeys - they take food, phones and glasses.
Motorcycles use the newer crossing; keep to the pedestrian side.
Alcohol and meat are prohibited in Rishikesh.

schedule.note: Temple hours; the riverside area is open longer

attractions.verification_note: Bridge closures and replacement crossings have changed since 2019 - verify current access before visiting.

attractions.name: Ram Jhula & Parmarth Niketan Aarti
attractions.summary: A 1986 suspension bridge linking the ashram bank to Swarg Ashram, beside the riverside Ganga Aarti at Parmarth Niketan.
attractions.history: Ram Jhula was built in 1986 to connect Sivananda Ashram with the Swarg Ashram quarter across the river. Parmarth Niketan, founded in 1942, sits on the eastern bank and conducts a daily sunset Ganga Aarti on its riverfront steps, led by resident students with Vedic chanting.
attractions.significance: The Parmarth aarti is the principal evening ritual in Rishikesh and is deliberately participatory - visitors sit on the steps among the ashram students rather than watching from a distance. The Swarg Ashram bank concentrates most of the town's yoga and meditation institutions.
interesting_facts: The aarti is led by children studying at the ashram's residential gurukul.
A large Shiva statue sits in the river directly in front of the ghat.
Vehicles are not permitted on the Swarg Ashram side, which keeps the riverside quiet.
Sitting on the steps to join the aarti is free and open to anyone.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The bridge deck is level but reached by steps at both ends; the aarti ghat is a stepped amphitheatre. A companion is advisable for anyone with limited mobility.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear removed on the aarti steps.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography of the aarti is permitted from the steps; be unobtrusive.
local_customs: Arrive at least 30 minutes early for a seat on the steps.
Remove footwear before stepping onto the ghat.
Alcohol and meat are prohibited in Rishikesh.

schedule.note: Aarti begins around sunset and runs roughly an hour

attractions.verification_note: Aarti timing follows sunset - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Beatles Ashram (Chaurasi Kutia)
attractions.summary: The abandoned Maharishi Mahesh Yogi ashram where the Beatles stayed in 1968, reopened in 2015 as a forest heritage site.
attractions.history: The Maharishi Mahesh Yogi established the Transcendental Meditation ashram here in the 1960s. The Beatles arrived in February 1968 and stayed several weeks, writing a large part of what became the White Album. The lease lapsed in 1997 and the site was reclaimed by Rajaji Tiger Reserve; it reopened to visitors in 2015 with the ruins and their later murals left in place.
attractions.significance: The ashram is where Indian meditation practice entered global popular culture. Its distinctive beehive-shaped meditation cells are an unusual piece of 1960s ashram architecture, and the murals added by later visitors have turned the ruins into an accidental open-air gallery.
interesting_facts: The Beatles wrote much of the White Album during their stay in early 1968.
The domed stone meditation cells were designed for solitary practice.
The site lay abandoned for nearly two decades before reopening in 2015.
It falls inside Rajaji Tiger Reserve, which is why entry is ticketed by the forest department.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Forest paths are uneven with roots, steps and steep sections between buildings. Not wheelchair accessible.
attractions.dress_code: No restriction; closed shoes recommended for forest paths.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; commercial shoots require forest department permission.
local_customs: Some buildings are structurally unsafe - stay on marked routes.
Do not deface the murals.
Elephants are occasionally present in this forest; follow staff instructions.

schedule.note: Forest department hours; last entry before closing

attractions.verification_note: Forest department hours and fees change seasonally, and the site closes in heavy monsoon - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Triveni Ghat
attractions.summary: The main bathing ghat in Rishikesh town, with a nightly Maha Aarti and a large fish population in the shallows.
attractions.history: Triveni Ghat takes its name from the symbolic confluence of the Ganga, Yamuna and the mythical Saraswati. It has long been the town's principal ritual bathing point and the site where pind daan ceremonies for ancestors are performed. The evening Maha Aarti here is older and less formalised than the ashram-run ceremonies upstream.
attractions.significance: Triveni Ghat is where local Rishikesh - as distinct from the ashram and rafting economies - conducts its ritual life. It is the main site for ancestral rites in the town and the most accessible of the ghats.
interesting_facts: The ghat's name refers to a symbolic meeting of three rivers.
Feeding the fish in the shallows is a local custom, and puffed grain is sold for the purpose.
Pind daan ancestral ceremonies are performed here throughout the year.
The ghat is level and open, making it the easiest riverside spot in Rishikesh to reach.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The upper terrace is level with vehicle access close by, making this the most wheelchair-friendly ghat in the twin towns. The water's edge is still reached by steps.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear removed on the ghat.
local_customs: Do not enter deep water - the current is strong even where it looks calm.
Alcohol and meat are prohibited in the town.
attractions.verification_note: Aarti timing follows sunset - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Mansa Devi Temple
attractions.summary: A hilltop Shakti temple reached by cable car or a stone footpath, with a wide view over Haridwar and the Ganga canal.
attractions.history: The temple on Bilwa Parvat is dedicated to Mansa Devi, a form of Shakti believed to fulfil the wishes of devotees. It forms part of the Panch Tirth circuit of Haridwar together with Chandi Devi, Maya Devi, Gangadwar and Kushwart. A ropeway was installed in the 1980s, greatly increasing visitor numbers.
attractions.significance: Mansa Devi is one of the two principal hilltop Siddhapeeths of Haridwar and the most visited. The wish-thread tradition - tying a thread to the temple tree and returning to untie it once the wish is fulfilled - is central to its practice.
interesting_facts: Devotees tie threads to a tree in the courtyard and return later to untie them.
The cable car covers the climb in a few minutes; the footpath takes 30-45 minutes.
The temple is one of five sites in Haridwar's Panch Tirth pilgrimage.
The summit gives the clearest overview of Haridwar's layout along the Ganga.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The ropeway avoids the climb but the upper station still has steps to the temple courtyard, and queue barriers are narrow. Not practical for wheelchair users.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear removed at the temple entrance.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography inside the sanctum is not permitted.
local_customs: Ropeway queues can exceed an hour on weekends and festival days.
Secure belongings from monkeys along the path.
Leather items are discouraged inside the temple.

schedule.note: Ropeway operates shorter hours than the temple

attractions.verification_note: Ropeway fares and operating hours change seasonally - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Chandi Devi Temple
attractions.summary: A Siddhapeeth on Neel Parvat across the river, traditionally established by Adi Shankaracharya, reached by ropeway or a 3 km trek.
attractions.history: The temple stands on Neel Parvat on the eastern bank of the Ganga. The principal image is traditionally said to have been installed by Adi Shankaracharya in the eighth century, with the present temple structure built in 1929 by the king of Kashmir, Suchat Singh. It is one of Haridwar's Panch Tirth.
attractions.significance: Chandi Devi is regarded as one of the three Siddhapeeths of Haridwar, where prayers are believed to be fulfilled. Its position on the opposite bank makes it noticeably quieter than Mansa Devi, and the trek up is a genuine walk through forest rather than a paved stair.
interesting_facts: The 3 km footpath from Chandighat is a real forest trek, not a stepped stair.
The temple is counted among Haridwar's three Siddhapeeths.
It is markedly less crowded than Mansa Devi across the river.
The Neel Parvat summit gives a view along the Ganga where it leaves the hills.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Either a ropeway with steps at both stations or a 3 km uphill forest trek. Not accessible.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear removed at the temple.
local_customs: Carry water if trekking; there is little shade on parts of the path.
Monkeys are common along the route.
attractions.verification_note: Ropeway operation is weather-dependent - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Neelkanth Mahadev Temple
attractions.summary: A Shiva temple at 1,330 m in dense forest about 32 km from Rishikesh, at the spot where Shiva is said to have swallowed the ocean's poison.
attractions.history: The temple marks the place where, in the Samudra Manthan narrative, Shiva consumed the halahala poison churned from the ocean, turning his throat blue - hence Neelkanth, 'blue throat'. The site has been a pilgrimage destination for centuries; the current temple structure with its carved gopuram-style entrance is more recent.
attractions.significance: Neelkanth is the most important Shiva shrine in the Rishikesh area and the focus of the Shravan month kanwar pilgrimage, when hundreds of thousands of devotees walk the route carrying Ganga water. The forest road approach through Rajaji National Park is itself a significant part of the experience.
interesting_facts: The temple sits at about 1,330 m, surrounded by dense forest on three sides.
During Shravan the road is closed to most vehicles as kanwar pilgrims walk the route on foot.
The approach passes through Rajaji National Park, where elephants are regularly seen.
A natural spring at the temple is used by pilgrims for ritual bathing before darshan.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The mountain road is winding with sharp bends, and the temple courtyard is reached by steps. Not accessible, and the journey is tiring for anyone prone to motion sickness.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear removed at the temple.
local_customs: Avoid during Shravan unless joining the pilgrimage - crowds are enormous.
The forest road can close after landslides in monsoon.
Do not stop for elephants on the park road; keep moving.

schedule.note: Sanctum closes for a midday break

costs.note: Free; forest road may carry a vehicle toll

attractions.verification_note: Road access is weather-dependent and heavily restricted during Shravan - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Ganga Whitewater Rafting (Shivpuri stretch)
attractions.summary: Grade II-IV rafting on the Ganga between Shivpuri/Marine Drive and Rishikesh, the most established commercial whitewater run in India.
attractions.history: Commercial rafting began on this stretch in the late 1980s and grew into India's largest whitewater market. The Uttarakhand government now licenses operators, sets safety standards and defines a seasonal window, with the river closed to rafting during the monsoon when flows are dangerous.
attractions.significance: This stretch is where organised adventure tourism in India effectively began, and it remains the standard training ground for Indian river guides. Rapids on the run carry established names - Three Blind Mice, Return to Sender, Roller Coaster, Golf Course.
interesting_facts: Rapids are graded II to IV depending on the stretch and season.
Rafting is officially suspended during the monsoon months for safety.
The most common commercial run covers roughly 16 km from Shivpuri to Rishikesh.
Operators must be registered with the state tourism department.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Requires scrambling down a riverbank to the put-in and the ability to swim and self-rescue. Not accessible.
attractions.dress_code: Quick-drying clothing, secured footwear. Helmet and life jacket are mandatory and supplied.
attractions.photography_policy: Operators supply photography; personal phones and cameras are best left ashore.
local_customs: Use only operators registered with Uttarakhand Tourism.
Rafting is closed during the monsoon - do not accept an operator who offers it.
Minimum age and swimming requirements apply and are enforced.
Alcohol before rafting is prohibited.

schedule.note: Rafting suspended by order during monsoon high flow

costs.note: Varies by stretch length and operator

attractions.verification_note: The operating season, permitted stretches and safety rules are set annually by the state - verify before booking.

attractions.name: Daksha Mahadev Temple
attractions.summary: An ancient temple in Kankhal marking the site of Daksha's sacrifice and Sati's self-immolation.
attractions.history: The temple in Kankhal, the oldest quarter of Haridwar, is associated with the puranic account of Daksha Prajapati's sacrifice, which Shiva was not invited to and at which his wife Sati immolated herself. The present structure dates largely to a 1810 rebuilding by Queen Dhankaur, with later additions.
attractions.significance: Daksha Mahadev is theologically central to the Shakti Peetha tradition, since Sati's death here initiated the sequence in which her body parts fell across the subcontinent. It is a principal site of Shravan-month worship and of the Kankhal pilgrimage circuit.
interesting_facts: Kankhal is considered older than Haridwar town itself.
A small pit in the courtyard is traditionally identified as the site of the sacrificial fire.
The temple is a major focus during the month of Shravan.
It is calmer than the central Haridwar ghats and worth pairing with them.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The main courtyard is largely level with a shallow step; the sanctum is raised.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear removed at the entrance.
local_customs: Leather items are discouraged inside.
Extremely crowded during Shravan.
attractions.verification_note: Timings change during Shravan - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Bharat Mandir
attractions.summary: The oldest temple in Rishikesh, traditionally re-established by Adi Shankaracharya in the ninth century.
attractions.history: Tradition holds that Adi Shankaracharya re-consecrated this Vishnu temple in the ninth century CE on the site of a much older shrine. The image in the sanctum is carved from a single black saligram stone. A small museum on the premises holds sculptural fragments and pottery recovered from the site.
attractions.significance: Bharat Mandir is the historical nucleus of Rishikesh town and predates the ashram belt entirely. Its Basant Panchami festival, when the deity is carried in procession, is the town's oldest continuous public ritual.
interesting_facts: The main image is carved from a single saligram stone.
Excavated pottery and sculpture from the site are displayed in a small on-site museum.
Circumambulating the temple three times on Akshaya Tritiya is a local tradition.
It is in the old town, away from the ashram and rafting crowds.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The courtyard is at street level; the sanctum has a raised threshold.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear removed at the entrance.
attractions.photography_policy: Sanctum photography is not permitted; the museum may allow it - ask first.
local_customs: Remove footwear at the marked line.
attractions.verification_note: Timings are not officially published - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Rajaji National Park (Chilla Range)
attractions.summary: A 820 sq km tiger reserve in the Shivalik foothills, best known for its elephant population; safaris run from the Chilla gate.
attractions.history: Three sanctuaries - Rajaji, Motichur and Chilla - were merged in 1983 to form Rajaji National Park, named after C. Rajagopalachari. It was declared a tiger reserve in 2015. The park spans the Shivalik foothills where the Ganga leaves the mountains, and forms the north-western limit of the Asian elephant's continuous range.
attractions.significance: Rajaji protects the north-western extreme of the Asian elephant's range and is an important corridor connecting Himalayan and Terai ecosystems. Its resident species include elephant, tiger, leopard, sloth bear, sambar and over 400 bird species.
interesting_facts: The park marks the north-western limit of the continuous Asian elephant range.
It was declared India's 48th tiger reserve in 2015.
Over 400 bird species have been recorded here.
The park closes entirely during the monsoon, from mid-June to mid-November.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Safaris use open jeeps on rough forest tracks, boarded by a high step. The ride is bumpy and long. Not suitable for wheelchair users or anyone with back problems.
attractions.dress_code: Muted colours, warm layers for early mornings, closed shoes.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; drones are strictly prohibited in the reserve.
local_customs: Safari permits must be booked in advance through the forest department.
The park is closed mid-June to mid-November.
Do not leave the vehicle or make noise near wildlife.
Elephants here can be aggressive - follow the guide's instructions exactly.

costs.note: Entry; jeep and guide charged separately

attractions.verification_note: Safari slots, permit rules and the seasonal closure are set by the forest department each year - verify before booking.
